1:
Whether the title fits the psalm is disputed at once. Adam Clarke says flatly that nothing in the contents bears any relation to it: by the title this should be a song of triumph, whereas the first part is a tissue of complaints of defeat. He presses two further objections, that it was not Joab who smote the Edomites but his brother, and that the number given elsewhere is eighteen thousand rather than twelve; and he offers a remedy, that the three opening verses of this psalm and of a later one should change places. Keil and Delitzsch notice the same discrepancy and answer differently: the inscription comes from a historical work which gave the psalm in this connection and is not taken from any history preserved to us. Matthew Henry takes the heading at its word and finds the double occasion in the psalm, since David is in care about the Syrians and rejoicing in his success against the Edomites; we have our cares at the same time as our joys, and they serve as a balance to each other. John Calvin reads the occasion politically, David being settled on the throne and exalting God’s goodness both to express gratitude and to conciliate those who still stood out, uniting a community rent into factions.

Augustine of Hippo turns the discrepancy into a principle. The prophetic Spirit in the psalm titles, he says, departs somewhat from the expression of things done and says something not found in the history, and by that departure admonishes us that such titles are written not that we may know things done but that things future may be prefigured. He sets the whole in his usual frame: David was one man but figured more than one, sometimes the Church gathered from the ends of the earth, sometimes the one Mediator.

Whether the calamity is military or political divides the rest. Charles Ellicott notes that the verb is used of a wall and elsewhere of the rout of an army, and quotes an English poet’s cry that they are broken, they are broken; yet the next two verses seem to him to describe a political convulsion rather than a military defeat, and he passes on a conjecture that a breach between two kingdoms is meant. On the next verse he would render land rather than earth, since though the image is an earthquake the convulsion described is political, not physical. John Wesley agrees in a clause: the trembling signifies great changes among the people. John Gill keeps earthquake and theology together: whatever natural causes there may be, it is always ascribed to God, and the land of Israel and not the whole earth is meant. C.H. Spurgeon reads the politics as piety: David traced the evil to its source, seeing the flight of Israel’s warriors, the breaking of her power and the division in her body politic as the hand of God — his were the politics of piety, which after all are the wisest and most profound.

C.H. Spurgeon also weighs what being cast off means. God has treated them as foul things to be put away, as beggarly persons to be shunned, as dead boughs torn from the tree; and to be cast off by God is the worst calamity that can befall a man or a people. But the worst form of it, he adds, is when a man is unaware of it and indifferent to it, for when the divine desertion causes mourning and repentance it will be but partial and temporary — when a cast-off soul sighs for its God it is not indeed cast off at all. John Gill refers the complaint forward instead, to the casting off of the Jews as a church and nation after they rejected the Messiah; Adam Clarke keeps it in the present, the reeling of drunken men in a land whose enemies prevail.
4:
What the banner is they answer at different levels. Adam Clarke keeps to the object, a sign capable of being fixed on a pole, and takes the verse to mean that God had appointed for his people a certain signal of favour, which David, standing before the oracle, prays to see proceed from it — a voice, perhaps joined with some luminous emanations, whence the phrase of the light of God’s countenance. John Wesley makes it an instrument of two things, union and battle: this people, lately divided, God has united under one banner and under David’s government, and given them power to oppose their enemies, a blessing granted for the sake of the few sincere Israelites among them. C.H. Spurgeon reads it as commission: their afflictions had led them to exhibit holy fear, and being so fitted for the Lord’s favour they were given an ensign which was at once a rallying point, a proof that he had sent them to fight, and a guarantee of victory. The bravest men are usually entrusted with the banner, he observes, and those who fear God most have least fear of man; the Lord has given us the standard of the gospel, and to publish it is a sacred duty while to be ashamed of it is a deadly sin. John Gill takes the banner for the Messiah himself, given for an ensign to the people, for the gathering of them to him and to show them where they should stand and whom they should follow.

John Gill also passes on a different construction, that a Jewish commentator took the word to signify temptation or trial, reading the verse as continuing the account of Israel’s distresses — troubles given them that they might be tried whether they would stand in the fear of God. Gill prefers a peculiar blessing bestowed on some while the rest lay under calamity.

The following clause is where the sharpest disagreement lies. Charles Ellicott holds that amid the uncertainty attaching to the verse one thing is certain, that the Authorised rendering of the second clause must be abandoned: for the word rendered truth we must read, with the Greek versions, the word for a bow; it is more than doubtful that the preposition can mean because of; and the rendering that it may be displayed cannot be defended. He would translate that God has given his fearers a banner, that they may rally to it from before the bow. Adam Clarke keeps truth and paraphrases: if they displayed the ensign and went out against enemies who had made such a breach among them, it was because of God’s truth, the promises of victory they supposed would attend them always; and he reports a rendering by another hand making the signal one displayed before the truth. John Wesley reads the same word as faithfulness, so that the blessing came not for any merit of theirs but to show God’s truth in making good his promises. C.H. Spurgeon presses that further: the truth of God was involved in the triumph of David’s armies, since he had promised them victory, and so in the proclamation of the gospel we need feel no hesitancy, for as surely as God is true he will give success to his own word.

On the petition that follows, John Gill takes the beloved not chiefly for Israel, chosen above all people on the earth, but for the elect among Jews and Gentiles, loved with a free and unchangeable love, who having fallen into condemnation and into the hands of many enemies could not work out their own deliverance. Charles Ellicott notes instead that from this verse onward the psalm appears again, with some variations, in a later psalm.
6:
Who speaks in these verses is the first question. Charles Ellicott holds that these three verses form the centre of the poem and are plainly of different age and authorship from the beginning, possibly an original poem by themselves, an ancient oracular saying about Israel’s bordering tribes, taken up by later compilers to rouse the drooping spirits of the race. On that reading the speaker is God himself, appearing after a familiar prophetic figure as a warrior, the captain of Israel, proclaiming the triumphs won by his might. Matthew Henry hears David instead, rejoicing in hope and praying in hope: God has given his word of promise and sworn by his holiness, and such are the triumphs of the saints, not so much for what they have in possession as for what they have in prospect. C.H. Spurgeon agrees and generalises: faith is never happier than when it can fall back upon the promise of God, since the voice of a faithful God drowns every sound of fear; and believers should banish doubts while promises remain.

What the oracle grants they set out much alike. John Gill canvasses where the speaking was done — in heaven, in the tabernacle by Urim and Thummim, by the prophets, or in the perfection of that holiness by which God swore — and applies the promise beyond David to his greater Son. Charles Ellicott prefers the reading in his sanctuary, which suits the utterance of an oracle, would render the next verb raise a shout of triumph, and takes what follows as implying unquestioned ownership, I may divide Shechem; Shechem and Succoth, he adds, mark the whole breadth of the country from west to east. John Wesley reads the pair the same way, one place within Jordan and one without, for all Canaan. C.H. Spurgeon makes the division an act of faith, which is sure of what God has promised and enters at once into possession. Adam Clarke keeps his own frame, that Judah shall not only be re-established in Jerusalem but possess Samaria and the land beyond Jordan, the tribes named being the material of one restored people.

The images of the last verse draw the fullest comment. Charles Ellicott takes the washpot for a footbath, a figure of great contempt, and illustrates it from the Egyptian king who broke up his golden footpan and had it made into an image of a god — a thing turned from base use to divine — as an allegory of his own rise from private person to king. He reports another explanation from Arabic proverbs, that the conqueror would as it were wash his face white in Moab, that is acquire renown there; and the comparison may have been prompted by Moab’s nearness to the Dead Sea, which lay at Israel’s foot. For the shoe he thinks the most natural sense is that Edom is disgraced to the character of the slave to whom the conqueror tosses his sandals to be cleaned, the custom of leaving sandals outside a temple door having fastened ideas of vileness on that article of dress. He adds that the received rendering of the Philistia clause cannot be what was intended.

John Wesley reaches the same conclusions briefly: the washpot means the lowest degree of servitude, the shoe is proverbial for using men like slaves, and the call to Philistia is ironical, her triumphs being come to an end. John Gill makes the vessel one for low and mean service and supposes great numbers of Moabites were then servants in Israel, employed like the Gibeonites as drawers of water to fill the pots in which hands and feet were washed. Adam Clarke reads the whole as prediction rather than record, the Moabites reduced to the meanest slavery and Idumea completely conquered, and points forward to the later prince who subdued the Edomites and compelled them to profess the Jewish religion.
9:
The question that opens these verses is a question about a fortress, and the commentators divide over which one. John Gill canvasses the options — some understand Rabbah of the Ammonites, which Joab besieged and to which he sent for David to come in person; the Targum interprets it of Tyre — but he judges it rather the same with Edom, the metropolis of the Edomites, since the next clause names Edom outright. Adam Clarke keeps his own frame, that this half of the psalm looks to the return of the captives from Babylon, and so allows a wider field: Petra, the capital of Idumea; Bozra, in Arabia near the mountains of Gilead; Rabbah; or Tyre, according to the Chaldee; or Jerusalem itself, which though dismantled had long been one of the strongest cities of the east. He also allows that the question may ask not for a city but for dominion over the countries already named.

Charles Ellicott settles the matter on the parallelism. The Hebrew wants the article, so any strongly fortified city might be meant, were it not that the next line names Edom; the strong city must therefore stand for Selah, or Petra, and he refers to Obadiah 1:3 for its impregnable position. He then explains why the asking is a real difficulty and not a flourish: there are only two possible approaches to the place, each a long narrow tortuous defile, and the city itself is so buried in its ravines that it cannot be seen from any spot in its neighbourhood, far or near. John Wesley reaches the same country by a shorter road, taking the singular for a plural — the strongholds left standing after the enemy has been beaten out of the field — and noting that Edom was high and rocky, fortified by nature as well as by art, and so not to be subdued without a divine hand.

C.H. Spurgeon reads the question as David’s own. The invading bands had been slain in the valley of salt, but the interior fortresses were not yet taken, and David meant to push his conquests to the city of the rock, deemed impregnable. From this he draws the lesson that great success must be a stimulus to greater efforts but not a reason for self-confidence: we must look to the strong for strength as much at the close of a campaign as at its beginning. No heights of grace are too elevated for us, the Lord being our leader, but high things attempted in self-reliance are another matter. Joab could not bring David into Edom, and the veterans of the valley of salt could not force the passage; yet it was to be attempted, and David looked to the Lord for help.

The following verse turns the question back on God, and the readings agree. Adam Clarke makes the point sharply: it is the very God who cast us off and abandoned us in battle from whom we expect complete enlargement, and we expect it because he has graciously promised these mercies. John Wesley hears the same reversal in a phrase, the God who had cut us off having now graciously returned to us. C.H. Spurgeon puts it as paradox: the chastising God is our only hope, for a small moment does he forsake but with great mercy does he gather his people, and he who is strong to smite is also strong to save. John Gill takes the question as an affirmation in disguise and carries it far forward, to the foretold destruction of the Romish antichrist — God is faithful to his purposes and promises, and strong is the Lord that judgeth Babylon; he will put it into the hearts of the kings of the earth to hate her and reward her double, and will call his people to rejoice at a fall as irretrievable as it is righteous.
11:
The closing plea is read at two distances. C.H. Spurgeon keeps it in the psalm’s own crisis: help us to overcome the disasters of civil strife and foreign invasion, from further incursions without and division within. The confession that follows he takes as hard-won rather than pious: we have painfully learned the utter impotence of armies, kings and nations without thine help, and our banners trailed in the mire have proven our weakness, but yonder standard borne aloft shall witness to our valour now that thou hast come to our rescue. Adam Clarke compresses the same movement into a sentence that is half confession: we have done all we can do, and have trusted too much in ourselves; now, Lord, undertake for us.

John Gill begins there and travels further. Trouble is the common lot of all men but especially of the people of God, who have troubles others have not — from indwelling sin, from Satan’s temptations, from the hidings of God’s face — and generally the greatest share of outward troubles besides, certain to them by the appointment of God and the legacy of Christ, needful and lying in their way to heaven. But he thinks a particular trouble is meant here: the time a little before the destruction of antichrist, great and none like it, the time of Jacob’s trouble out of which he shall yet be saved, the slaying of the witnesses and the hour of temptation that will try the Christian world. Then, as in all their troubles, the saints will seek to the Lord for help, which he has promised and gives seasonably, and which is owing wholly to his own grace and goodness.

The last verse raises the question of what is left for men to do once God treads the enemy down. C.H. Spurgeon states the principle plainly: from God all power proceeds and all we do well is done by divine operation, yet we, as soldiers of the great king, are to fight, and to fight valiantly. Divine working is not an argument for human inaction but rather the best excitement for courageous effort; helped in the past we shall be helped in the future, and being assured of this we resolve to play the man. For the treading down he keeps both hands in view: like straw beneath the feet of the oxen shall we tread upon our foes, but it shall rather be his foot which presses them down than ours. From him the might proceeds, to him the honour is given. John Gill reads the clause with the Targum as through the Word of the Lord, and makes that Word Christ, appearing at the head of his armies in a vesture dipped in blood and a sharp sword proceeding out of his mouth, inspiring his people to fight valiantly under him and winning in his own strength the victory over the beast, the false prophets and the kings of the earth.

Adam Clarke agrees in a line — through thee alone shall we do valiantly, thou alone canst tread down our enemies — and then leaves the verse. Returning to an authority cited earlier in the psalm, he reproduces in the original Latin an eyewitness account of the Crusaders at Jerusalem: some three hundred Saracens took refuge on the roof of the Temple of Solomon and would not come down until they received Tancred’s banner as a pledge of protection — and were killed to the last man. Clarke records that Tancred was filled with indignation and about to avenge the breach of faith when the chiefs intervened, maintaining not only the expediency of the massacre but the necessity of putting every remaining inhabitant to the sword. Of what followed he translates only the beginning before stopping: I can translate no farther; it is too horrible.
